vignette:
He is 45 now, a quiet African man who works long days as an agricultural worker, moving steadily through rows of crops with the kind of endurance that makes him easy to overlook. He speaks softly, often after a pause, as if he is measuring whether a memory can be safely touched. When he talks about his childhood, he begins not with himself but with the house: the small rooms, the heat that collected indoors at night, the way everyone could hear everything. He grows up in a home where violence between his parents is never far away. As a boy, he learns to read danger from sound before he can make sense of it in words—the scrape of a chair, his father’s footsteps, his mother’s sudden silence.

The worst nights come without warning. He remembers lying awake, staring into the dark, waiting for the first crash. Sometimes it is shouting, then pleading, then the unmistakable sound of blows landing. Sometimes he sees it directly: his father towering over his mother, his mother trying to shield herself, younger children crying in the corner. He wants to intervene, but he is small and terrified. On more than one occasion he freezes completely, feeling his heart pound so hard he thinks someone else must hear it. He tells himself to stay still, to keep the younger ones quiet, to be ready in case they need to run. In those moments he feels both intensely alert and strangely absent, as if part of him has slipped away to survive what the rest of him cannot bear.

By daytime he tries to act like other children. He goes to school, helps with chores, keeps his eyes on adults’ moods. But he carries a constant tension in his body. He startles easily when someone raises a hand too quickly or when voices sharpen nearby. He begins sleeping lightly, waking at small noises, then struggling to return to sleep because once he is awake his mind replays what he has seen. He rarely talks about any of it. In his family and community, hardship is something people endure, not describe. He learns to lock things away and to be useful.

As he gets older, that usefulness becomes his identity. He works early, first helping others with land and animals, later finding steady work in agriculture. He likes the predictability of physical labor: planting, lifting, cutting, watering. Out in the fields, there is a rhythm he can trust. He knows what to do with his hands, and the body can be exhausted in an honest way that sometimes quiets his mind. Even so, certain sounds pull him out of the present. A metal tool slamming onto the ground can send a shock through him. Angry voices from another part of the farm make his stomach tighten before he even knows why. He scans faces quickly, watching for signs that tempers are changing. Coworkers sometimes experience him as reserved or overly serious. They do not see the effort it takes for him to feel safe enough to stay.

In his relationship, the past enters in more private ways. He cares deeply for his partner and wants closeness, but conflict unsettles him beyond what he thinks it should. If she sounds frustrated or raises her voice, he feels his chest constrict and his thoughts race. He may go silent, leave the room, or stay outside longer than necessary, telling himself he just needs air. Later he feels ashamed, knowing she is speaking to him, not attacking him, but in the moment his body reacts as if he is back in that childhood house. He says he hates arguments not because he fears being wrong, but because he is certain that once anger starts, something terrible follows.

Sleep remains one of his biggest struggles. He has recurring dreams in which he hears his mother crying out and is unable to move. On some nights he wakes sweating, already on edge, and checks the doors and windows before lying back down. His partner has noticed that he thrashes in his sleep and sometimes wakes suddenly, breathing hard. During the day he is often tired, but rest does not come easily. He avoids films, conversations, and family gatherings that might bring up scenes of domestic conflict. If neighbors are fighting, he turns up the radio or leaves. Still, avoidance does not protect him for long; memories intrude anyway, vivid and sensory, especially when he is tired or stressed.

What troubles him most in the present is not only the memories, but the enduring feeling that danger is always near. Even in the fields, under open sky, he listens for signs of trouble. He prefers positioning himself where he can see who is approaching. He keeps his own anger tightly controlled because it feels too close to what he witnessed. He has spent much of his life trying to be the opposite of the man he feared, yet the fear itself remains, living in his body. He says he has worked hard, loved carefully, and built a life that looks steady from the outside. But inside, part of him is still that boy in the dark, listening for the first sound that tells him the night is about to turn.
